title: Zeroth Fitting ideal of a direct sum
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M,N$ be finitely generated $R$-modules [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Write $I_0(P)$ for the zeroth kernel-minor ideal of a finite free surjection onto any finitely generated $R$-module $P$, independent of that surjection by [lem-trf-fitting-ideal-independence-base-change]. Then
$$I_0(M\oplus N)=I_0(M)I_0(N).$$

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07ZA (lemma-fitting-ideal-basics), part (2), the equality Fit_0(M direct sum N) = Fit_0(M) Fit_0(N).

proof.text: Choose finite generating families of $M$ and $N$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], giving surjections $\pi:R^{\oplus n}\to M$ and $\rho:R^{\oplus m}\to N$ by sending the standard coordinates to those generators. Put $K=\ker\pi$ and $L=\ker\rho$. The map $q:R^{\oplus(n+m)}\to M\oplus N$, $q(x,y)=(\pi(x),\rho(y))$, is surjective, since preimages can be chosen separately, and $\ker q=K\oplus L$, since $q(x,y)=0$ exactly when $\pi(x)=0$ and $\rho(y)=0$. The combined family $(\pi(e_i),0),(0,\rho(e_j))$ generates $M\oplus N$. Thus [lem-trf-fitting-ideal-independence-base-change], with $k=0$, computes $I_0(M)$, $I_0(N)$ and $I_0(M\oplus N)$ from these three surjections. Write their kernel-row ideals as $A$, $B$, $C$, respectively.

source.place: Tags 07Z8 (lemma-fitting-ideal), kernel-row description, and 07ZA (lemma-fitting-ideal-basics), proof of (2): the direct-sum presentation.

proof.text:
For a generator of $C$, take $n+m$ rows $z_i=(x_i,y_i)$ in $K\oplus L$ and form the square matrix $Z=[X\ Y]$ with the first $n$ and last $m$ columns separated. In the Leibniz sum [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], group permutations according to the set $S$ of rows used in the first $n$ columns. If $S=\{s_1<\cdots<s_n\}$ and its complement is $\{t_1<\cdots<t_m\}$, every permutation in this group is uniquely $\tau_S\circ(\alpha\oplus\beta)$, where $\tau_S$ lists $s_1,\ldots,s_n,t_1,\ldots,t_m$ and $\alpha\in S_n$, $\beta\in S_m$. Its sign is $\operatorname{sgn}(\tau_S)\operatorname{sgn}(\alpha)\operatorname{sgn}(\beta)$. Distributing the two finite sums therefore gives
$$\det Z=\sum_{|S|=n}\operatorname{sgn}(\tau_S)\det(X_S)\det(Y_{S^c}).$$
Here $X_S$ consists of $n$ rows of $K$ and $Y_{S^c}$ of $m$ rows of $L$, in increasing order. Hence their determinants belong to $A$ and $B$. Each summand belongs to the product ideal $AB$, and so $C\subseteq AB$. This is a regrouping of the defining finite sum, not an appeal to an unstated minor-ideal formula.

source.place: Tag 07ZA (lemma-fitting-ideal-basics), proof of (2), expanding the determinant calculation behind Tag 07Z7 (lemma-ideals-generated-by-minors), part (4).

proof.text: Conversely, let $a=\det(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ and $b=\det(y_j)_{j=1}^m$ be kernel-row generators of $A$ and $B$. The rows $(x_i,0)$ followed by $(0,y_j)$ lie in $K\oplus L$. In the Leibniz sum [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] for their block diagonal matrix, a term is zero unless its permutation preserves the two blocks. The remaining permutations are uniquely pairs $(\alpha,\beta)\in S_n\times S_m$, with product signs; distributing gives determinant $ab$. Thus $ab\in C$. Every $u\in A$ and $v\in B$ is a finite linear combination of their respective determinant generators, so distributing $uv$ writes it as a finite linear combination of such $ab$. By the definition of ideal multiplication as finite sums of products $uv$, this proves $AB\subseteq C$. Together with Step 2 and the identifications of Step 1 this is the asserted equality. If $n=0$ or $m=0$, the empty determinant is $1$ by the same cited definition: the subset and permutation sums above still apply, including $n=m=0$. No finite generation of $K$ or $L$ was used.

source.place: Tag 07ZA (lemma-fitting-ideal-basics), proof of (2), reverse inclusion in the block-diagonal maximal-minor calculation of Tag 07Z7(4), with empty blocks included.

proof_origin.place: Tags 07ZA (lemma-fitting-ideal-basics), part (2), and 07Z8 (lemma-fitting-ideal), kernel-row description. The determinant expansion omitted in 07Z7(4) is written out directly using the Leibniz formula.
